rules.title: Proposed ban on algorithmic rent-setting devices (Prohibition of Anti-Competitive Automated Rent Price-Fixing Ordinance)
rules.requirement: Landlords could not use software that analyzes nonpublic competitor data to set rents or occupancy levels for residential rental property in San Diego, and no one could sell or license such software to landlords. A tenant could sue the landlord for an injunction, damages, or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, plus attorney's fees.
rules.key_value: Ban on sale, licensing and landlord use of algorithmic devices using nonpublic competitor data; up to $1,000 civil penalty per violation, with each month and each property counted as a separate violation
rules.coverage_conditions: All residential rental property in the City of San Diego (as defined in SDMC § 98.0702); applies to landlords using algorithmic devices and to any person selling, licensing or providing them to landlords.
rules.exemptions: Software that publishes reports from aggregated nonpublic competitor data more than 90 days old, or from public information, and does not recommend rents or occupancy levels for future leases or renewals; software used to set rents or income limits under local, state or federal affordable housing program guidelines.
rules.quoted_span:
(b) It is unlawful for a landlord to use an algorithmic device to set rental rates
or occupancy levels for residential rental property.
rules.penalty: Tenant civil action for injunctive relief, damages, or civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation; each month and each property is a separate violation; mandatory costs and reasonable attorney's fees to a prevailing tenant; remedies are cumulative; SDMC Ch. 1, Art. 2 enforcement also applies.

exemption_tests.description: Software used to set rents or income limits under local, state or federal affordable housing program guidelines

rules.conflict_note: This document is the staff report and draft ordinance (O-2025-107). The ordinance number, date of final passage and adoption certification are all blank. Its effective date is set as 30 days after final passage, but no passage date appears. Adoption, and any later amendment, should be checked against the City Clerk record before treating this as in force. A reviewer should also check whether state law on common pricing algorithms (Cartwright Act amendments) affects this local ban.

notes: The document is the San Diego staff report (Feb 27, 2025), draft ordinance O-2025-107, the City Attorney digest and the strikeout version. They all contain the same text, so I extracted one rule, covering both the ban on selling or licensing the software (§98.1103(a)) and the ban on landlords using it (§98.1103(b)). Status is 'pending' because the document shows no adoption: the ordinance number, date of final passage and clerk certification are blank. My background knowledge suggests the City Council may have adopted it in 2025, but this document does not show that. If adopted, the status should be in_force, with the effective date 30 days after final passage. The document also mentions San Francisco's 2024 ban and Philadelphia's ordinance. I did not extract those: the San Francisco one is only referenced in passing with no supporting text, and Philadelphia is out of scope.
